title: Complexity and the Array · control flow, functions, errors (Lecture 02, Lab 02)

questions.stem: f(n) = 3n2 + 5n + 2 is:
questions.explanation: Keep the fastest-growing term, drop its constant: 3n2 → n2. It is also O(n3), but not Θ(n3) (c) — Θ is a tight bound.

questions.stem: Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: n ≤ 1 · n2 for all n ≥ 1. O is an upper bound, so a slower-growing function is O of a faster one. (a) and (d) put a faster function under a slower one; (b) claims n grows at least as fast as n2.

questions.stem: f(n) = O(g(n)) means:
options: there are constants c > 0 and n0 with f(n) ≤ c · g(n) for all n ≥ n0
f(n) = g(n) for all large n
there are constants c > 0 and n0 with f(n) ≥ c · g(n) for all n ≥ n0
questions.explanation: Constants you choose, and only from some n0 on. (b) has no constant and no n0; (c) is equality, not a bound; (d) is the definition of Ω.

questions.stem: In the worst case, how many comparisons does linear search make on an array of n elements?
questions.explanation: Worst case: the target is last or absent, so every element is compared once.

questions.stem: The target is present and equally likely to be at any of the n positions. On average, how many comparisons does linear search make?
questions.explanation: (1 + 2 + … + n)/n = (n+1)/2. Still O(n) — half is a constant.

questions.stem:
What is the running time of this loop?

i = n
while i > 1:
    i = i // 2
questions.explanation: Halving until 1 takes about log2 n steps. Θ(n/2) (d) would be subtracting, not dividing — and it is just Θ(n) anyway.

questions.stem:
What is the running time?

for i in range(n):
    for j in range(i):
        count += 1
questions.explanation: 0 + 1 + … + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2. The answer must be a function of n only, so (c) is not an answer.

questions.stem:
What is the running time?

for i in range(n):
    for j in range(5):
        count += 1
questions.explanation: The inner loop is a constant 5: 5n = Θ(n). Nested loops multiply their iteration counts, not their nesting depth.

questions.stem: For a Python list of n items, x in values costs:
options: O(1), because lists are hash tables
questions.explanation: A list is an array; in checks items one by one. Sets and dicts are the hash tables (a).

questions.stem: Which Python list operation is O(1) (amortised)?
questions.explanation: append writes at the end — nothing moves — and the occasional resize averages out (Week 4). The other three shift or search: O(n).

questions.stem: Why is reading a[i] from an array O(1)?
options: Python caches the last element read
The array searches from both ends at once
The slots are contiguous and equal-sized, so the address is base + i × slot size
questions.explanation: Address arithmetic. It has nothing to do with order (a) or caching (b).

questions.stem: A partly filled array has size 6. How many elements must move to insert a new value at index 2?
questions.explanation: Slots 2, 3, 4, 5 move right: size − index = 6 − 2 = 4.

questions.stem: When inserting into an array, the elements after the gap must be shifted right. In which order?
options: From the insertion index towards the end
From the last used slot back towards the insertion index
Any order — the result is the same
Swap each element with its neighbour, from the front
questions.explanation: Moving right, start at the right, or you overwrite values before you move them (see W2-S2).

questions.stem: a = Array(4), then a[-1]. What happens?
questions.explanation: The course Array has no negative indices, like C.

questions.stem: a = Array(5), then a[0] = 7. What is len(a)?
questions.explanation: len is the capacity, fixed at creation. Tracking how many slots are in use is your job.

questions.stem: A 3 × 4 matrix (3 rows, 4 columns) is stored flat in row-major order. At which index is element (2, 1)?
questions.explanation: r × cols + c = 2 × 4 + 1 = 9.

questions.stem: What extra space does reverse_in_place(arr) need (swap from both ends, no second array)?
questions.explanation: Two indices and one temporary for the swap, whatever n is.

questions.stem: Under the course storage rule (Lecture 02), which of these is not allowed?
options: a Stack storing its items in the student's own DynamicArray
a Graph storing adjacency in the student's own ChainingHashMap
a queue class storing its items in a Python list
bfs returning the visit order as a Python list
questions.explanation: A structure may not store its data in a Python list. (a) and (b) build on the student's own structures — allowed; (d) is a list used as a return value — the interface, allowed.

questions.stem: Python's built-in list is best described as:
options: a fixed-size C array of integers
a hash table keyed by position
a dynamic array of references to objects
questions.explanation: A block of references plus a size and a capacity; it grows by copying into a bigger block.

questions.stem: An O(n) loop is followed by an O(n2) loop. The whole is:
questions.explanation: Sequence adds: O(n + n2) = O(n2).

questions.stem:
values is a Python list of n items. The cost of:

for i in range(len(values)):
    if values[i] in values[i + 1:]:
        return True
questions.explanation: Each iteration hides two O(n) operations: the slice copies up to n items and in searches them. n iterations of O(n) work.

questions.stem: When does the else block of a for loop run?
options: Whenever the loop body raises an exception
Only if the loop runs zero times
When the loop finishes without executing break
questions.explanation: Think of it as "no break".

questions.stem:
Given

def f(a, L=[]):
    L.append(a)
    return L

what does f(1) then print(f(2)) print?
questions.explanation: The default list is created once, when def runs, and shared by every call that uses it.

questions.stem: What is the value of 0 or 'x' and ''?
questions.explanation: and binds tighter: 0 or ('x' and ''). 'x' and '' gives '' (the last value looked at); 0 or '' gives ''.

questions.stem: list(range(2, 11, 3)) is:
questions.explanation: Start 2, step 3, stop before 11: 2, 5, 8.

questions.stem:
What does print(g()) print?

def g():
    try:
        return 1
    finally:
        print("bye")
questions.explanation: return 1 is decided, then finally runs (printing bye) before the function actually returns; then print shows 1.

questions.stem: In the RAM model of Lecture 02, which of these is not one basic step?
options: x in values on a Python list of n items
calling a function (the call itself, not what it then does)
questions.explanation: in on a list walks it comparing item by item, O(n) — a hidden loop (Rule 5). One slot read or write (a), one comparison of small numbers (c) and the call itself (d) each take constant time.

questions.stem: An algorithm does n2 basic steps and takes 1 second at n = 10,000. About how long will it take at n = 100,000, on the same machine?
questions.explanation: Ten times the input, squared: 102 = 100 times the work, so about 100 seconds. 10 seconds (a) is what an O(n) algorithm would take; 1,000 (b) would be n3.

questions.stem: Algorithm A does 1000n steps; algorithm B does n2 steps. Which statement is true?
options: B does fewer steps for n < 1,000; A does fewer for every n > 1,000
A does fewer steps for every n, because O(n) beats O(n2)
B does fewer steps for every n, because its constant is 1
They are equally good, because both are polynomials
questions.explanation: 1000n < n2 exactly when n > 1000. Big-O describes growth for large n, so (b) is wrong for small n; (c) ignores that n2 overtakes any 1000n; being polynomials (d) says nothing about which is smaller.

questions.stem: Which sentence about linear search is correct?
options: Its worst case is Θ(1), because Θ describes the best input
Big-O means "worst case" and Big-Ω means "best case"
Its best case is Θ(1) and its worst case is Θ(n)
It does exactly n comparisons on every input of size n
questions.explanation: "Best/worst case" says which input; O, Ω, Θ say what kind of bound. The two are independent, so (a) and (b) confuse them. (d) is false: it stops at the first match, so one comparison is enough when the target is first.

questions.stem:
What is the running time of this loop?

i = 0
while i * i < n:
    i += 1
questions.explanation: The loop stops when i2 ≥ n, that is after about √n steps (n = 1,000,000 gives i = 1,000). It neither halves (a) nor walks all the way to n (c).

questions.stem: A recursive total(values) makes one call per element and creates no new data. Its extra space is:
options: O(1), because it creates no new data
O(n), because every call that has not returned keeps a frame on the call stack
questions.explanation: Recursion uses space: n calls deep means n frames waiting at once. Creating no data (a) is not the same as using no memory — and Python stops at about 1,000 frames.

questions.stem: A partly filled Array has size 7. How many elements move during remove_at(arr, 7, 2)?
questions.explanation: Slots 3 to 6 move left: size − index − 1 = 7 − 2 − 1 = 4. Five (b) is the count for insert_at at index 2.

questions.stem: remove_at ends with arr[size - 1] = None. Why?
options: So that len(arr) goes down by one
Without it, the shifted values would end up in the wrong order
That slot is no longer in use; clearing it removes a stale copy of the last value, which would otherwise keep that object alive
The course Array raises an error if a slot is not None
questions.explanation: After the shift, slot size - 1 still holds a copy of the last reference. Clearing it means nothing reads a stale value, and the object can be freed. len(arr) is the fixed capacity and never changes (a); the order (b) was already right after the shift.

questions.stem: In C, after int a[6];, the statement a[6] = 0;:
options: raises an index error at run time
makes the array grow to 7 slots
is the same as a[0] = 0, because indices wrap round
writes past the end with no check, over whatever is stored next — a buffer overflow
questions.explanation: C does not check indices: a[6] is base + 6 × 4, the memory right after the array. No error is raised (a), and an array cannot grow (b) or wrap (c). The course Array checks, and raises IndexError.

questions.stem: One Python array can hold an int, a str and a list, and still index in O(1). Why?
options: Python sorts the objects by size first
Each slot holds a reference, and all references are the same size
Python pads every object to the size of the largest one
It cannot: indexing is O(1) only when all items have the same type
questions.explanation: The slot holds a reference to the object, not the object; every reference is 8 bytes on a 64-bit machine, so base + i × 8 still works. The objects themselves live elsewhere, at any size — no sorting (a) or padding (c).

questions.stem: a = Array(3), then a[0:2]. What happens?
options: TypeError: the course Array does not support slicing
a new Array of two Nones is returned
questions.explanation: A slice is a copy, O(k), dressed as one step, so the course Array refuses it: "Array does not support slicing; copy with a loop".

questions.stem: arr holds [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. What does it hold after rotate_left(arr, 8)?
options: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] — 8 is more than a full turn, so nothing moves
questions.explanation: rotate_left first does k %= n: 8 mod 6 = 2, so it rotates left by 2. (a) would be right only for k = 6 or 12; (d) is a rotation to the right by 2.

questions.stem: merge_sorted(a, b) takes the front of a when a[i] <= b[j]. Why <= rather than <?
options: With <, the result would not be sorted
With <, two equal values would raise an error
With <, the loop would never end on equal values
With <=, equal values keep their order — the one from a first — which merge sort relies on to be stable
questions.explanation: With <, an equal value from b would be taken first, swapping the order of equal values; the output would still be sorted (a), with no error (b) and no endless loop (c). Keeping equal values in their original order is stability (Week 10).

questions.stem: A 3 × 4 matrix holding the values 0 to 11 row by row is stored flat in row-major order. transpose_flat(arr, 3, 4) returns the 4 × 3 transpose, also row-major. At which index of the result is the value 1?
questions.explanation: 1 is at (0, 1) in the 3 × 4 matrix, so at (1, 0) in the 4 × 3 transpose: 1 × 3 + 0 = 3. The result is [0, 4, 8, 1, 5, 9, …].

questions.stem: "Any sort that works only by comparing elements needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case." This means:
options: no comparison sort can have a worst case below a constant times n log n; counting sort escapes only because it does not compare
every sorting algorithm, counting sort included, is at least n log n
every comparison sort does exactly n log n comparisons
comparison sorts are O(n log n) in the worst case
questions.explanation: It is a lower bound on the problem for comparison sorts. Counting sort (Week 9) uses the values as indices and never compares, so the bound does not apply to it (b). Ω is "at least", not "exactly" (c), and not an upper bound (d).

questions.stem: How many pairs does is_sorted(arr) compare when arr holds [5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8]?
questions.explanation: It compares 5 with 1, finds them out of order and returns False at once: O(1), the best case. Seven (a) is the number of pairs in a sorted array of 8.

questions.stem:
What happens when increment() is called?

count = 0

def increment():
    count = count + 1
questions.explanation: The assignment makes count local for the whole function, so reading it on the right-hand side finds a local with no value yet. Python does not fall back to the global (a, c), and the error is more specific than a NameError (b).

questions.stem:
What does print(users) show?

users = ['guest1', 'guest2', 'ali', 'guest3']
for u in users:
    if u.startswith('guest'):
        users.remove(u)
print(users)
options: RuntimeError: the list changed size during iteration
questions.explanation: Removing 'guest1' shifts every item left, so the loop's next position holds 'ali': 'guest2' is skipped. 'guest3' is then removed. A list does not raise (d) — dicts and sets do. Loop over a copy, or build a new list.

essays.stem: Big-O throws away constant factors and lower-order terms. Explain why each is thrown away, give one situation where doing so is misleading, and explain how measuring complements counting.
essays.answer:
• Lower-order terms stop mattering as n grows: in 1/2 n2 - 1/2 n, the n2 term is 99.9% of the total by n = 1,000.
  • Constant factors are not properties of the algorithm: they change with the machine, the language and how you count steps. What stays the same everywhere is the shape of growth.
  • Misleading when n is small, or constants are huge: a 1000n algorithm is worse than an n2 one for every n < 1,000; linear search beats binary search on tiny arrays.
  • Measuring (viz.complexity.measure) shows the constants and the crossover point that Big-O hides; counting shows the shape that one machine's timings cannot prove. You need both.

essays.stem: Define O, Ω and Θ precisely. For f(n) = 3n2 + 2n, give one true statement using each, and one true but uninformative O statement.
essays.answer:
• f = O(g): there exist c > 0, n0 with f(n) ≤ c g(n) for all n ≥ n0 — an upper bound.
  • f = Ω(g): there exist c > 0, n0 with f(n) ≥ c g(n) for all n ≥ n0 — a lower bound.
  • f = Θ(g): both — c1 g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2 g(n) eventually — a tight bound.
  • For 3n2 + 2n: it is O(n2), Ω(n2), Θ(n2); it is also Ω(n). True but uninformative: 3n2 + 2n = O(n3) (or O(2n)).

essays.stem: Describe the best, worst and average case of linear search, with the number of comparisons for each. Which one does "linear search is O(n)" usually refer to, and why is that the default?
essays.answer:
• Best: the target is the first element — 1 comparison, O(1).
  • Worst: last or absent — n comparisons, O(n).
  • Average (present, uniformly placed): (n+1)/2, still O(n) — and the average needs a stated assumption about the inputs.
  • "Linear search is O(n)" means the worst case: it is a guarantee that holds for every input of size n, needs no assumption, and is what you plan capacity around.

essays.stem: Explain why indexing an array is O(1) but inserting into the middle is O(n). What does the fact that an array has a fixed size force you to do when it fills up, and what does that cost?
essays.answer:
• An array is contiguous, equal-sized slots, so the address of a[i] is base + i × size: one multiplication and one addition, independent of n → O(1).
  • Inserting at index i in an array of size n needs every element from i to the end moved one place right: n - i moves, n in the worst case → O(n).
  • Fixed size: the memory after the block may belong to something else, so the array cannot grow in place. When it is full, you must allocate a new, larger array and copy every element across: O(n) for that operation.
  • (Doubling the capacity each time makes appends O(1) amortised — Week 4.)

essays.stem: State the course storage rule from Lecture 02. Give the reason for it, list what remains allowed, and show how two structures from later in the course follow it.
essays.answer:
• Rule: a data structure in dsa/ stores its data only in the course Array, in node objects, or in another structure the student has built — never in a Python list, dict, set or deque.
  • Reason: those built-ins hide exactly the costs the course teaches — one short call like insert(0, x), pop(0) or x in values is an O(n) algorithm someone else wrote. Building on a bare array makes every cost visible and yours.
  • Still allowed: lists as function inputs and return values; lists in tests; plain local variables and tuples.
  • Examples, any two: Stack on the student's DynamicArray; CircularQueue on an Array; ChainingHashMap as an Array of Entry chains; Graph on the student's hash map and DynamicArrays; MinHeap on a DynamicArray.

essays.stem: Compare Python's list, array.array, numpy.ndarray and a ctypes array on: can it grow, what it holds, and whether it hides costs. Why is the course Array built on ctypes?
essays.answer:
Grows?HoldsHides the cost?
listyes (dynamic array)references to any objectsyes
array.arrayyespacked numbers of one typeyes
numpy.ndarraynopacked numbers of one typeyes — whole-array operations run in C
ctypes arraynoC values or referencesno — index and assign only

A ctypes array of object references is a genuine fixed-size C array that can hold any Python object. The course wraps it, adds bounds checking, and offers nothing else — so every other operation must be written, and priced, by the student.

essays.stem:
values is a Python list of n numbers. Give the running time of each numbered part of this function, justify each with one of the five rules, and give the total. Why is part (3) not O(n2), although it hides a slice and an in inside a loop?

def report(values):
    total = 0
    for v in values:                 # (1)
        total += v
    i = len(values)
    while i > 1:                     # (2)
        i //= 2
    for v in values:                 # (3)
        if v in values[:10]:
            total -= v
    return total
essays.answer:
• (1) One pass over n items with an O(1) body: Rule 2, Θ(n).
  • (2) i is halved until it reaches 1: Rule 4, Θ(log n).
  • (3) n iterations (Rule 2); the body hides a slice and an in (Rule 5), but the slice copies at most 10 items and in searches at most 10 — a constant, not n. So the body is O(1) and the loop is Θ(n). A hidden loop costs what it actually walks: here a fixed 10, not the whole list.
  • Total, by Rule 1: Θ(n + log n + n) = Θ(n). (Timing it confirms this: doubling n doubles the time.)

essays.stem: Define the auxiliary space of an algorithm. Give the extra space of reverse_in_place, resized(arr, 2n), merge_sorted(a, b) and a recursive total(values), with a reason for each. Why does recursion use space even when it creates no data, and what limit does Python put on it?
essays.answer:
• Auxiliary space: the memory an algorithm needs beyond its input, as a function of n.
  • reverse_in_place: two indices and a swap — O(1). resized(arr, 2n): a new array of 2n slots — O(n). merge_sorted(a, b): the output array — O(n + m).
  • Recursive total(values): O(n) — every call that has not yet returned keeps a frame (its arguments, its local variables, where to return to) on the call stack, n frames at the deepest point.
  • Python stops recursion at about 1,000 frames (RecursionError), so a recursion n deep fails for large n; a loop with O(1) space does not. Time and space can be traded: merge sort uses O(n) extra space for its O(n log n) time.

essays.stem: Explain row-major order. A 5 × 7 matrix (5 rows, 7 columns) is stored flat in row-major order: at which flat index is element (3, 4), and which (row, column) is at flat index 30? Why is reaching (r, c) still O(1)?
essays.answer:
• Row-major: the rows are stored one after another in one flat array, so element (r, c) is at index r × cols + c.
  • (3, 4) in a 5 × 7 matrix: 3 × 7 + 4 = 25. Index 30: row 30 // 7 = 4, column 30 % 7 = 2, so (4, 2).
  • Reaching (r, c) is one multiplication and one addition, then one O(1) array index — whatever the matrix size.

essays.stem: The course Array refuses negative indices, slicing and append. For each refusal, explain why it is deliberate and what you write instead. Then explain the difference between len(a) and the size of a partly filled array, and who keeps track of each.
essays.answer:
• No negative indices: an index is an offset from the base, and there is nothing before the base (as in C). You compute size - 1 for the last element; DynamicArray (Week 4) adds negative indexing as the translation i + size.
  • No slicing: a slice is a copy, O(k), that looks like one step. You write the copying loop and see the cost.
  • No append: an array cannot grow; that is the definition. To make room you allocate a bigger Array and copy — resized, the dynamic array's one move.
  • len(a) is the capacity, fixed when the Array is created; the size — how many slots from index 0 hold real data — is kept by your code, in a separate variable (insert_at and remove_at take it and the caller updates it). That split is what the dynamic array is built on.
